# Members, initialization and extension boundaries

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `dotnet-members-inheritance` · **C# & .NET Runtime** · Catalog level: foundation

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S01-Q006](#S01-Q006)

<p>How do an abstract class and an interface express an extension point? Explain the contract and shared behavior before deciding which fits a library requirement.</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Design a C# type whose storage, accessibility and extension rules express a clear caller contract.</p>

<ul>
<li>Choose member storage and initialization from the requirement.</li>
<li>Trace overloading, overriding and shared behavior through a hierarchy.</li>
<li>Verify accessibility and class/interface forms in the target language version.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>A type first exposes state and behavior to callers. Initialization determines when that state is established, while accessibility and inheritance determine who may use or extend it; the questions follow those related contract boundaries.</p>

<a id="S01-Q003"></a>

### S01-Q003 · Foundation

<p>What is the difference between a field and a property in C#? Which would you expose for state that may later need validation?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q003](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q003)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q003](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q003)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What is the difference between a property and a field?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare stored state with a member access contract. Explain what a caller depends on and what an implementation may need to change.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose a public member shape while preserving a clear state contract.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use an ordinary class and a hypothetical evolving API; distinguish direct storage, auto-properties and custom accessors.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connects the choice to validation, mutability and caller expectations.</li>
<li>Shows a small API change and identifies compatibility or surprising side effects.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Saying a property is just a field with different syntax.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would make a property getter surprising or expensive for callers?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q012"></a>

### S01-Q012 · Foundation

<p>What does “class types” mean in your C# answer, and how would you compare the class forms relevant to that scope?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q012](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q012)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q012](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q012)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What class types are available in C# and how do they differ?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Resolve the source’s broad wording first. Then explain how forms such as ordinary, abstract, sealed and static classes express different intended uses.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Define an ambiguous classification and connect it to design intent.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Start with class modifiers, not all .NET types; state the language version and check official documentation before adding version-specific forms.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>States the chosen classification and relates each form to an instantiation or extension requirement.</li>
<li>Uses a small example to justify one form and its limitation.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Listing many language keywords without defining the classification or why it matters.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>Which form would fit a type that must not be extended, and how would you verify that choice?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q016"></a>

### S01-Q016 · Foundation

<p>How does an abstract class differ from an ordinary concrete class? Use a small hierarchy to explain the responsibilities of the base and derived types.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q016](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q016)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q016](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q016)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare an abstract class with a regular class.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare whether a type represents a complete usable implementation or an extension contract. Keep this question separate from the interface comparison.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Describe the responsibilities of an incomplete base implementation.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use ordinary C# classes and instance members; establish which behavior is shared and which a derived class must provide.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Shows an instantiation and extension example that matches the declared class intent.</li>
<li>Explains when adding a base abstraction would create more complexity than useful structure.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming an abstract class is merely a class containing no implemented methods.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>When would you keep a concrete class instead of introducing a base hierarchy?</li>
</ul>

</details>

### S01-Q006 · Foundation

<p>How do an abstract class and an interface express an extension point? Explain the contract and shared behavior before deciding which fits a library requirement.</p>

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare the contract that implementations must satisfy with the implementation or state they may share. Tie the choice to a concrete change requirement.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Defend an abstraction choice with a relevant alternative.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State the C# and runtime versions and check official documentation for supported interface features before relying on them.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains implementation sharing, inheritance constraints and consumer expectations using one example.</li>
<li>Identifies a requirement that would favor the alternative and tests substitutability.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Using an outdated slogan about interfaces without establishing the target language version.</li>
</ul>

<a id="S01-Q007"></a>

### S01-Q007 · Mechanism

<p>How do virtual and abstract methods differ when a derived class supplies behavior? Trace a call through a base-typed reference.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q007](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q007)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q007](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q007)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare virtual methods and abstract methods.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Explain the implementation obligation and the dispatch of a method call. Dispatch means selecting which implementation handles the call.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Predict method behavior across an inheritance boundary.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use ordinary instance methods in a named C# hierarchy; keep method hiding separate from overriding.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces the chosen implementation and required derived-class work in a small example.</li>
<li>Explains how an extension preserves the base contract and how to test that contract.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Describing both keywords as identical ways to replace a method.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would your example show if a derived method hid rather than overrode the base method?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q014"></a>

### S01-Q014 · Mechanism

<p>Which accessibility rules apply to interface members in the C# version you are targeting? Show how you would check a declaration and its implementation.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q014](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q014)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q014](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q014)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain accessibility rules for interface members.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Distinguish the interface’s contract from how a class exposes its implementation. The question requires a version-specific scope before applying a remembered rule.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Verify interface-member legality and caller visibility.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State the language version and member form, including any body or static modifier; consult official C# documentation for those exact forms.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Separates valid declarations, implementation requirements and access through different caller types.</li>
<li>Uses compilation and documentation to check a boundary example.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Repeating “all interface members are public” without qualifying the member form and language version.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<li>What changes in caller access if an implementation is explicit?</li>

<a id="S01-Q015"></a>

### S01-Q015 · Mechanism

<p>What problem would you use a static constructor to solve? Explain the initialization boundary and what you would investigate if initialization failed.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q015](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q015)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q015](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q015)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What is a static constructor used for?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Focus on type-level setup and the consequences of placing work there. Do not describe it only as a constructor with the static keyword.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Reason about initialization ownership and failure impact.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State the runtime, type and initialization form; consult official documentation before asserting precise triggering, concurrency or failure behavior.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces the proposed initialization and identifies observable failure effects.</li>
<li>Justifies why this boundary suits the work and considers a simpler explicit initialization path.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Putting blocking or fragile external work in initialization without discussing its failure boundary.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What evidence would distinguish a type-initialization failure from an ordinary method failure?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q018"></a>

### S01-Q018 · Mechanism

<p>Compare overriding and overloading in C#. How would you predict which method is called when declared and actual object types differ?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q018](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q018)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q018](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q018)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare overriding and overloading.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Separate choosing a method signature from choosing an implementation. Trace the call using the exact types available at each decision point.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Predict method selection without conflating two mechanisms.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use ordinary statically typed calls in a small class hierarchy; state if generics, dynamic or optional arguments enter the example.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces an overloaded and an overridden call with explicit declared types.</li>
<li>Demonstrates an edge case and explains the maintenance risk of an unclear overload set.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Using overriding and overloading as interchangeable names for changing a method.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you reduce ambiguity in an API with several similar overloads?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q013"></a>

### S01-Q013 · Application

<p>What boundary does internal accessibility express in C#? How would you use it when deciding which library members consumers may depend on?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q013](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q013)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q013](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q013)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain `internal` accessibility.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Explain access from the consumer’s location, not from a folder diagram. Relate that boundary to the public contract you are willing to maintain.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Design an intentional accessibility boundary for a library.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a library with separate consuming assemblies; state any friend-assembly arrangement before predicting access.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Predicts access for callers inside and outside the stated boundary.</li>
<li>Explains a maintainability benefit and distinguishes access control from data-security guarantees.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Treating internal as a namespace restriction or a security boundary.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would tests access implementation details without accidentally enlarging the public API?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q017"></a>

### S01-Q017 · Application

<p>Which combinations and uses of abstract, sealed and static classes are valid in your target C# version? Explain how the restrictions express design intent.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q017](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q017)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q017](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q017)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain restrictions involving `abstract`, `sealed`, and `static` classes.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Check both compiler legality and the requirement behind a declaration. A list of forbidden combinations does not explain why a class should use one of them.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Connect class restrictions to an intentional extension boundary.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name the language version and exact declarations; check official documentation and compiler diagnostics instead of extending rules to unrelated member forms.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Tests representative valid and invalid declarations with clear expected intent.</li>
<li>Explains the consequence for instantiation or inheritance without applying one rule to every type form.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Memorizing modifier combinations while ignoring the reason to restrict extension.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What simpler declaration would meet the same requirement?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q001"></a>

### S01-Q001 · Trade-offs

<p>When would you choose const rather than static readonly for a C# value? Explain the consequences when a shared library changes that value.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q001](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q001)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q001](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q001)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What is the difference between `static readonly` and `const`?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare the value’s initialization and the contract seen by code that consumes it. This asks about observable behavior, not which keyword looks shorter.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose a member declaration from initialization and compatibility requirements.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a hypothetical public library and consuming application; state whether both are rebuilt and redeployed together.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Predicts behavior for unchanged and rebuilt consumers with a small example.</li>
<li>Explains the requirement that would change the declaration and a way to check it.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Calling both declarations simply immutable without explaining initialization or consumer compatibility.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would you test if the library ships independently of its consumers?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A hypothetical public library exposes configuration and a replaceable calculation policy. Sketch the member declarations and extension contract, trace a base-typed call, and compare an interface with an abstract base. Check invalid declarations, initialization failure and independent consumer updates in the stated language/runtime version.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Explains members and class forms and predicts a concrete caller’s behavior.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Connects initialization, visibility and dispatch to compatibility, extension costs and targeted checks.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>A valid declaration or folder organization alone does not demonstrate a stable library contract.</p>
